summary: PIM-SM is a multicast routing protocol that can use the existing unicast routing table or a separate multicast one. It builds one-way shared trees rooted at a Rendezvous Point for each group, and can optionally switch to shortest-path trees. This revised specification updates the earlier PIM-SM documents.

eli5.summary: To share a video with many viewers, routers set up a meeting point first, and then everyone can use the shortest path between them and the sender.

subtitle: How routers deliver multicast traffic to groups of receivers by meeting at a Rendezvous Point and then optionally taking shortcuts.

tldr.problem: Multicast traffic has to get from sources to receivers across wide-area networks, even though neither side knows the other exists in advance.
tldr.mechanism: Receivers' routers send Join messages hop by hop towards a Rendezvous Point (RP) for the group, building a shared tree. Senders' routers register with the RP, and routers can then optionally switch to a shortest-path tree for each source.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7761 is an Internet Standard (STD 83) that replaces RFC 4601, is meant to interoperate with it, and drops a few features that lacked deployment experience.

today: RFC 7761 is an Internet Standard (STD 83) and obsoleted RFC 4601. It has been updated by RFC 8736 and RFC 9436.

sections.title: What PIM-SM Is
sections.content:
Protocol Independent Multicast - Sparse Mode (PIM-SM) is a protocol for efficiently routing multicast groups that may span wide-area and inter-domain internets. It is called protocol independent because it may use the underlying unicast routing for reverse-path information when building trees, but does not depend on any particular unicast routing protocol.

The Abstract describes it as building unidirectional shared trees rooted at a Rendezvous Point (RP) per group, and optionally creating shortest-path trees per source.

PIM-SM version 2 was first specified in RFC 4601 as a Proposed Standard. RFC 7761 specifies the same protocol, addresses reported errata, and removes the optional (*,*,RP) state, the PIM Multicast Border Router (PMBR) features and authentication using IPsec, because they lacked sufficient implementation and deployment experience (Appendix A, citing a survey in RFC 7063). Implementations of RFC 7761 are expected to interoperate with RFC 4601 implementations.
sections.eli5: PIM-SM is the set of rules routers follow so that one sender can reach many viewers without anyone having to know each other beforehand.

sections.title: Key Terms and State
sections.content:
The RFC defines a handful of terms the rest of the document relies on.

  • The Rendezvous Point (RP) is the router configured as the root of the non-source-specific tree for a group. Receivers' Joins go towards it, and senders' data goes to it.
  • The Designated Router (DR) is the one router elected per interface that acts for directly connected hosts.
  • The MRIB (Multicast Routing Information Base) is the multicast topology table, usually derived from the unicast routing table or from a protocol such as MBGP. It decides where Join/Prune messages are sent.
  • The RPF neighbor is the neighbor the MRIB says to use to reach an address. RPF means Reverse Path Forwarding.
  • The TIB (Tree Information Base) holds the state created by Join/Prune messages, Assert messages and IGMP or MLD information from local hosts. The MFIB is the efficient forwarding table a real router builds from it.

TIB state comes in three kinds: (*,G) state for the shared tree of group G, (S,G) state for a source-specific tree, and (S,G,rpt) state for source-specific information on the shared tree, such as a prune of a source that is now arriving by the shortest path. The state is an abstract description: an implementation may store it any way that produces the same externally visible behavior.
sections.eli5: Think of a school bus system: the RP is the central bus station, the DR is the one bus driver in charge of each street, and the MRIB is the map that says which way to go to get somewhere.

sections.title: The Three Phases of Building a Tree
sections.content:
Senders and receivers can come and go at any time, so the three phases below may all be happening at once.

Phase one: the RP tree. A receiver expresses interest in a group, typically using IGMP or MLD. Its DR sends a (*,G) Join towards the RP. Each router the Join passes creates tree state for group G, until it reaches the RP or a router that already has that state. Together the Joins form the RP tree, also called the shared tree. Joins are resent periodically, and a DR sends a Prune when the last receiver leaves. A sender simply starts sending: its DR unicast-encapsulates the packets in Register messages and sends them to the RP, which decapsulates them and forwards them down the shared tree.

Phase two: Register-Stop. Encapsulation is costly, and the path via the RP can be long. So the RP normally sends an (S,G) Join towards the source S. When the packets start arriving natively, the RP discards the encapsulated copies and sends a Register-Stop to the source's DR.

Phase three: the shortest-path tree. A router on the receiver's LAN, typically the DR, may optionally send an (S,G) Join towards S. When traffic arrives over the shortest-path tree (SPT), that router drops the copies arriving over the RP tree and sends an (S,G,rpt) Prune towards the RP.

On multi-access LANs, duplicate Joins can lead to duplicate traffic. PIM does not prevent this. Instead, routers notice duplicate data and elect one forwarder with Assert messages.
sections.eli5: First everyone meets at a central spot to find each other. Then the sender's helper tells the spot to stop carrying every parcel, and finally the viewers can take a straight road to the sender instead of the detour.

sections.title: Hello, Register, Join/Prune and Assert
sections.content:
Hello and DR election. Routers must send Hello messages on all active PIM interfaces, including point-to-point links, to the ALL-PIM-ROUTERS group (224.0.0.13 for IPv4, ff02::d for IPv6). Hellos are also how options are negotiated. The DR Priority option (default priority 1) is a 32-bit number and the larger value wins, with the higher IP address breaking ties. If any neighbor omits the option, the router with the higher IP address wins. A GenID option holds a random 32-bit value that changes when forwarding restarts, so neighbors can detect reboots. Neighbors ignore Join/Prune and Assert messages from a router they have not yet heard a Hello from.

Register. The DR encapsulates packets from local sources to the RP until it receives a Register-Stop. It then starts a Register-Stop Timer, and just before the timer expires it sends a Null-Register to let the RP refresh the Register-Stop. If the timer actually expires, the DR resumes encapsulating.

Join/Prune. Join/Prune messages are sent towards the upstream neighbor to build and tear down shared and source trees. The RFC specifies state machines for the downstream and upstream side of each of the (*,G), (S,G) and (S,G,rpt) kinds of state.

Assert. When a router receives a data packet on an interface where it would normally forward that packet, it can send an Assert. The router with (S,G) state wins; otherwise the better metric towards the RP or the source wins.

Switching to the SPT. Whether a last-hop router switches is a policy function, SwitchToSptDesired(S,G), that the implementation defines. An infinite-threshold policy never switches, and a switch-on-first-packet policy switches once a single packet has been received.
sections.eli5: Routers say hello to their neighbors every so often and pick one leader per street. Leaders ask for traffic with Join messages, and if two neighbors both send the same thing, they argue it out with Assert messages until only one keeps sending.

sections.title: Finding the Rendezvous Point
sections.content:
Every PIM router in a domain must map a given group to the same RP. If they do not, black holes can appear where some receivers cannot get some groups. The RFC does not mandate one mechanism. It lists four, each with problems: static configuration (which every PIM router MUST support), Embedded-RP (the RP address is encoded in an IPv6 multicast group address), Cisco's Auto-RP (which has no standard specification), and the Bootstrap Router (BSR) mechanism.

With the BSR mechanism, one router in the domain is elected BSR. Candidate RPs unicast their candidacy to it, and the BSR floods its chosen RP-set through the domain. A router maps a group to an RP in four steps: find the longest matching group range, keep the highest-priority RPs, use the single remaining RP, or, if several remain, use the PIM hash function to choose one.

The RFC also requires that any RP address that is configured, learned or advertised be reachable from all routers in the PIM domain.
sections.eli5: Every router in town has to agree on which central bus station a given group uses, otherwise some riders end up at the wrong station. There are a few ways to share that list, like writing it down by hand or electing one router to announce it.

sections.title: PIM Packet Formats
sections.content:
All PIM control messages use IP protocol number 103. Some are unicast, such as Register and Register-Stop. Others are multicast with TTL 1 to the ALL-PIM-ROUTERS group, such as Join/Prune and Assert. Every message starts with a common header: PIM version (2), message type, a reserved byte and a 16-bit checksum. A message with an unrecognized version or type, or sent to the wrong kind of destination, MUST be discarded.

The Hello message carries options such as Holdtime, whose value is in seconds. A Holdtime of 0xffff means the receiver never times the neighbor out, and a Holdtime of zero is a goodbye that tells receivers to drop the neighbor immediately.

A Register message has a Border bit (deprecated here: set to 0 and ignored) and a Null-Register bit, followed by the original multicast packet. Its checksum covers only the first 8 bytes. A Join/Prune message names an upstream neighbor, a holdtime, and for each group a list of joined and pruned sources. An Assert carries a group, a source, a Metric Preference and a Metric, plus an R bit that is 1 for (*,G) asserts and 0 for (S,G) asserts.
sections.eli5: Every PIM message begins with the same small label saying which kind it is, and then the details specific to that kind follow.

sections.title: Source-Specific Multicast
sections.content:
The Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) service model can be built from a strict subset of PIM-SM. It uses a reserved range of group addresses, currently 232.0.0.0/8 in IPv4 and ff3x::/32 in IPv6, and the group address alone decides whether SSM or ordinary semantics apply.

For a group in the SSM range, a router MUST NOT send (*,G) or (S,G,rpt) Join/Prune messages, MUST NOT send Register messages, and MUST NOT forward on (*,G) or (S,G,rpt) state. An RP MUST NOT forward Register-encapsulated packets for an SSM address and SHOULD answer them with a Register-Stop.

An implementer may build a PIM-SSM-only router. It needs the Hello and DR election logic, the packet forwarding rules, the upstream and downstream (S,G) state machines and the (S,G) Assert state machine. It does not need the Register state machine, the (*,G) and (S,G,rpt) state machines, bootstrap RP election, the Keepalive Timer or the SPTbit.
sections.eli5: In source-specific mode a viewer names exactly which sender they want, so there is no need for a central meeting point at all.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
PIM relies on an MRIB populated outside of PIM, so the RFC recommends securing the sources of change to the MRIB. It then separates two kinds of forged messages.

Link-local messages (Join/Prune, Hello, Assert) are not forwarded by a compliant router, so they can only come from a local host or a compromised or non-compliant router. A forged Join can waste bandwidth, a forged Hello can make an attacker the DR, and a forged Assert can make the legitimate forwarder stop forwarding to the LAN.

Register and Register-Stop messages travel by normal IP forwarding, so an attacker anywhere in the network may forge them. A forged Register can make the RP inject forged traffic onto the shared tree, and a forged Register-Stop can stop a DR from registering packets. These do not apply to PIM-SSM-only implementations.

A router SHOULD offer an option to limit which neighbors it accepts Join/Prune, Assert and Hello messages from. A DR MUST NOT register-encapsulate a packet unless its source address is legal for the receiving subnet. Authentication of link-local messages is covered by RFC 5796, and denial-of-service attacks such as sending to many groups quickly or forging many Joins can still consume router resources.
sections.eli5: Because routers mostly trust the messages they hear from neighbors, a liar on the same network could make traffic go to the wrong place or stop. The RFC suggests only listening to known neighbors and checking that senders are using proper addresses.

messages.label: (*,G) Join
messages.note: Sent hop by hop towards the RP; builds the shared tree.

messages.label: Register
messages.note: Source data is unicast-encapsulated to the RP.

messages.label: (S,G) Join
messages.note: RP joins towards the source so data can arrive natively.

messages.label: Register-Stop
messages.note: Sent once native packets arrive, so encapsulation stops.

items.desc: Unicast to the source of the Register.

items.desc: Used in PIM-DM only; unicast to RPF'(S).

items.desc: Used in PIM-DM only; unicast to the source of the Graft.

fields.desc: Set to zero on transmission and ignored on receipt.
